Earlier we spoke about the disjointed letters (al-huruf al-muqatta'a) at the beginnings of some surahs of the Qur'an. Here we will only note that these disjointed letters, such as (Qaf), represent the unseen (al-ghayb) aspect of the Qur'an, and the unseen is the touchstone of faith, as we have explained.

Consider the unlettered farmer, for example, who uses the television and switches between its channels without knowing how it works or how it moves from one channel to another. He benefits from it without knowing how it operates. Likewise, he uses the water pump (al-tulumba), and he does not know its mechanics.

Similarly, with these disjointed letters, we believe in them and leave their meanings to the One who spoke them, glory be to Him. Religion divides into three elements: beliefs that build up the hearts; acts of worship and obligations, which are the work of the limbs; and then speech that conveys all of these matters, which is the task of the tongue, that is, expression.

Each of beliefs, obligations and expression contains both the unseen and the seen. God is unseen, but the traces of His power in the universe are seen. Prayer, in terms of your going to the mosque five times a day and what it includes of bowing, prostration and movements, is seen, but the number of its units (rak'at) is unseen.

It is as if the Truth, glory be to Him, gives us the unseen in these matters in order to test the reality of faith within us. What you know is evidence for the truth of what you do not know.

The same applies to the letters and verses of the Noble Qur'an. We generally understand the verses of the Qur'an and know their meanings, but the disjointed letters are the unseen which we must believe in even if we do not know their meaning. These letters remain evidence of the inimitability of the Qur'an (i'jaz al-Qur'an).

His saying, exalted be He: ﴿Qaf. By the glorious Qur'an﴾ [Qaf: 1] combined the two: the unseen in (Qaf) and the seen in ﴿and the glorious Qur'an﴾ [Qaf: 1]. These are the two components of the Noble Qur'an: (Qaf) is the evidence of its inimitability, and ﴿the glorious Qur'an﴾ [Qaf: 1]. So He brought the proof and that which is proven by it.

(Qaf) carries the meaning of an oath. It is a single letter, just as God swears by a single thing, when He says: ﴿By time, indeed mankind is in loss﴾ [al-'Asr: 1-2], and He says: ﴿By the star when it sets, your companion has neither strayed nor erred﴾ [al-Najm: 1-2].

He also swears by two letters, such as (Ya Sin), (Ta Ha), (Ha Mim), and He likewise swears by two of His creatures, such as: ﴿By the morning brightness, and by the night when it is still﴾ [al-Duha: 1-2]. He swears by three letters, such as (Alif Lam Mim), and by three things, such as: ﴿By those who line up in rows, then those who drive away with a driving, then those who recite the reminder﴾ [al-Saffat: 1-3].

He swears by four in ﴿Alif Lam Mim Sad﴾ [al-A'raf: 1], and in ﴿By the fig and the olive, and Mount Sinai, and this secure land﴾ [al-Tin: 1-3]. He swears by five letters in ﴿Kaf Ha Ya 'Ayn Sad﴾ [Maryam: 1], and in His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿By the Mount, and a Book inscribed, on parchment unfolded, and the much-frequented House, and the raised canopy, and the swelling sea﴾ [al-Tur: 1-6].

So this oath came in five patterns, from one up to five, and it did not exceed that so that the oath would not be burdensome on the tongue, and because the most a bare word can contain is five letters. But in swearing by His cosmic signs, He went beyond that.

Read: ﴿By the sun and its brightness, and by the moon when it follows it, and by the day when it displays it, and by the night when it covers it, and by the heaven and He who built it, and by the earth and He who spread it, and by the soul and He who proportioned it﴾ [al-Shams: 1-7].

Had He done the same in swearing by letters, it would have departed from the structure of the word in the language.

We also note that the oath by the disjointed letters comes only at the beginnings of surahs, whereas the oath by the cosmic signs comes at the beginning, as we have seen, and also comes within the surah, as in His saying, exalted be He: ﴿Nay, by the moon, and by the night when it withdraws, and by the dawn when it brightens﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 32-34].

Then, the oath by the disjointed letters does not take the particle wa (and). The oath particle wa comes with the other verses whose meaning is understood. Here He says: ﴿Qaf. By the glorious Qur'an﴾ [Qaf: 1], and He did not say "wa Qaf," because wa is a letter and Qaf is a letter, and that would create ambiguity (labs) between them. This is one of the inimitable aspects of the Qur'an that we should pause at and reflect upon.

Affirming these unseen matters is what establishes the truthfulness of faith. Otherwise, what is the advantage in every verse of the Qur'an being understood, with its meaning and purpose known? What is the advantage in every matter of religion being known to us, subject to rational analogy (al-qiyas al-'aqli) and having evidence for it?

We have previously clarified that the seen and belief in the seen is an ordinary matter, everyone believes in it. The important thing is that you believe in what is hidden from you, out of trust in the one who informed you of it.

Suppose you went to the doctor, and after he examined your condition, he prescribed a medicine. By God, would you debate with him, asking why he wrote this and why he wrote that? You do not debate him, because you went to him by choice. You went to him trusting him, and ready to carry out his instructions and take the medicine he prescribed for you, while you know nothing about it.

If you trust the doctor, who is a human being like me and like you, and subject to error, then what about God? Will you not trust His words?

Because of the importance of faith in the unseen, God praised the believers in it, saying: ﴿who believe in the unseen...﴾ [al-Baqarah: 3]. Just as we believe in the verses whose meaning is clear, we believe in the letters whose meaning is not clear. So this is a Qur'an of the seen and this is a Qur'an of the unseen, and just as we believe in the observable cosmic signs, we believe in God, their Creator and Originator, who is unseen, glory be to Him.

As for His saying, exalted be He: ﴿and the glorious Qur'an﴾ [Qaf: 1], "the Qur'an" is the name of what was sent down from God upon the heart of our master, the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and it indicates his truthfulness in conveying it. It was named Qur'an to indicate that it is read (maqru'), and it was named Kitab to indicate that it is written (maktub). It is recorded in lines and preserved in hearts.

The Qur'an has a special distinction not given to any book before it: the Qur'an carries both the method (al-manhaj) and the miracle together. As for the earlier messages, the method was in the book, while the miracle was separate from it.

Our master Jesus, for example, had the Gospel as his book, and his miracle was that he healed the blind and the leper and brought the dead to life by God's permission. Our master Moses had his book and method in the Torah, but his miracle was in the staff. As for our master, the Messenger of God (ﷺ), his miracle was the very same as his method. Why?

Because his message is lasting and remains throughout all time until the Hour, and remains across all place. It has the universality of time and the universality of place. Now we can say: "This is Muhammad, the Messenger of God, and this is his miracle," whereas we cannot say that about our master Moses or our master Jesus, for example, because their miracles ended with the ending of their times.

The meaning of ﴿al-Majid﴾ [Qaf: 1] is: the Mighty, possessor of honour, glory and exaltedness. Majid is on the pattern fa'il, which is one of the intensive patterns, like rahim (very merciful). Fa'il sometimes comes in the sense of the active participle, like rahim meaning raahim (one who shows mercy), and sometimes in the sense of the passive participle, like qatil meaning maqtul (one who is killed).

So the meaning of ﴿al-Majid﴾ [Qaf: 1] is: glorious in His essence and glorified in His essence. Both meanings are carried: He is glorious (majid) and glorified (mumajjad). Because it is the highest and most elevated speech, and the most precious and noblest of books, it is glorious in itself.

Then, because it came from the Most High Glorious One, the Truth, glory be to Him, and was conveyed by a glorious angel to a glorious Messenger, and in addition it was sent down upon a glorious community.

But if: ﴿Qaf. By the glorious Qur'an﴾ [Qaf: 1] is an oath, where is its response? They said: it is an oath that the Resurrection is true; that is: "Qaf, by the glorious Qur'an, you will surely be resurrected." The closer view is to take the response from the statement following the oath, which is His saying, exalted be He:

﴿Rather, they wonder that a warner has come to them from among themselves...﴾.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 50, verse 2:

Wonder (al-ʿajab) arises only from something unusual, whose cause and reason the soul cannot discern, like the sorcerer: we wonder at what he does because we do not understand it. The discussion here concerns the disbelievers contemporary with the mission of the Prophet (ﷺ).

The Qur'an has clarified and explained this matter in another place, the saying of God Most High: ﴿And they say, "Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a man of importance from the two cities?"﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 31]. ﴿And they say, "Why has an angel not been sent down to him?" And if We had sent down an angel, the matter would have been decided, and they would not be reprieved. And if We had made him an angel, We would have made him a man and would have confused them as they confuse themselves﴾ [al-An'am: 8-9].

So, their wonder or objection is not directed at the Qur'an, but at Muhammad (ﷺ): how can the Qur'an be sent down to him when he is one of the common people? And why was it not sent down to one of the great men of the people? Then they came up with another doubt: why was it not sent down to an angel?

The Qur'an has responded to them and explained this doubt to them. Muhammad (ﷺ) is a messenger and a model (qudwah), and modelling is not complete unless the messenger is of the same kind as those to whom he is sent. Otherwise, how could we follow an angel who has a nature different from our nature and a power different from our power?

If we were commanded to do some deed, it would not be proper for us to say to him: "We cannot do what you do, because you are an angel who is able to do what we are not able to do." Thus the exemplary conduct (uswah) would not be complete.

Among the greatness of the message is that the messenger be one of you. Therefore God bestowed this favour upon them, saying: ﴿There has certainly come to you a messenger from among yourselves...﴾ [al-Tawbah: 128], i.e., of your kind, indeed of your own people, and one of the closest of people to you, and you know his truthfulness and trustworthiness even before the message, and you bore witness to that.

And the saying of God Most High: ﴿So the disbelievers said, "This is a strange thing."﴾ [Qaf: 2].

This means: it was the disbelievers who wondered at the choice of Muhammad (ﷺ) for the message. Therefore, those other than the disbelievers did not wonder at that. Since the Qur'an was sent down over a period of thirteen years, there were people who believed in Muhammad and confirmed him from the very first verse sent down to him, and he said: "Today there was sent down to me such-and-such."

Indeed, our master Abu Bakr confirmed the Messenger of God and believed in him merely when he said, "I am the Messenger of God," without asking him about anything. Why?

Because his past among his people qualified him for this rank. And why would he not confirm him, when he was the truthful one about whom no lie had ever been tested, and one who does not lie to the creatures is more worthy of not lying against the Creator?

Likewise he confirmed him concerning the report of the Night Journey and the Ascension, and did not dispute as others did, but said of the Messenger of God: "If he said it, then he has spoken the truth." He took it by reason, and by the premises he had from the biography of the Messenger of God.

Therefore the very name "Muhammad" is itself evidence of his truthfulness. In the saying of God Most High: ﴿Muhammad is the Messenger of God...﴾ [al-Fath: 29], "Muhammad" is the subject (mubtada'), of which the predicate is that he is the Messenger of God. And "Muhammad" means "the one praised" (mahmud), whom people praise and commend.

So he, from his beginning and upbringing, was prepared for this mission. Therefore they never tested a lie against him at all, nor anything of what his peers did in the Jahiliyyah. It is as if he says to them: "Muhammad is this man whom you know, and you know his past and his conduct among you; he is the Messenger of God." It is as if the reason for faith in the Messenger is that he is Muhammad.

And we have already explained how God preserved him from error? And how He preserved him from the exposure of his nakedness (awrah)? Therefore there came upon his tongue (ﷺ), while he was disputing with his people: ﴿I have already dwelt among you a lifetime before it. Will you not reason?﴾ [Yunus: 16].

This means: you know everything about me; you know that I do not lie, and that I have never stood up to speak as an orator or poet among you. So why do you deny me?

The phrase ﴿This is a strange thing﴾ [Qaf: 2] is not a repetition of the wonder in ﴿Rather, they wondered...﴾ [Qaf: 2]; rather, it is "strange" concerning what was said. The disbelievers said it, and the Qur'an explained it in the saying of God Most High: ﴿And what prevented the people from believing when guidance came to them was only that they said, "Has God sent a human as a messenger?"﴾ [al-Isra': 94].

So He replied to them: "What do you want?" They said: "We want him to be an angel." He said to them: "If he were an angel, he would come to you in the form of a man." Thus the doubt would remain as it is.

Here the matter shifted from objecting to the Messenger's humanity to casting doubt on the resurrection after death. Thus we have two answers to the oath ﴿Qāf. By the glorious Qur'an﴾ [Qāf: 1].

The first answer: "Indeed you are a warner." The second: "You will surely be resurrected." We took the first from His words: ﴿But they wonder that a warner has come to them from among themselves..﴾ [Qāf: 2], and the second from His words, glorified be He: ﴿When we have died and become dust? That is a far-off return.﴾ [Qāf: 3].

The meaning of ﴿a far-off return﴾ [Qāf: 3] is: a return to life after we die and become dust. This is a matter far from their minds. Why? Because you have among you the traces of our master Ibrahim and Isma'il, and the remnants of the earlier religions; you know God and acknowledge that He is your Creator and the Creator of the heavens and the earth.

In the story of our master Ibrahim, peace be upon him, the Qur'an relates his words: ﴿Ibrahim said, "My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead." He said, "Have you not believed?" He said, "Yes, but so that my heart may be at rest..."﴾ [al-Baqarah: 260].

We have said that the question here is not a doubt from our master Ibrahim about God's power to revive the dead; it is only a question about the how: ﴿how You give life to the dead..﴾ [al-Baqarah: 260].

So God, glorified be He, showed him the how, not as a saying but as an action and an experienced observation, which he himself tried, as if God, exalted be He, were saying to him and to us: the giving of life to the dead is neither difficult nor beyond My capacity. Rather, when I wish to extend My power to one of My servants, he does it by My permission. ﴿He said, "Take four birds and make them incline toward you; then place a part of them on every hill, then call them, and they will come to you in haste. And know that God is Mighty and Wise."﴾ [al-Baqarah: 260].

This is one of the signs of God's power, which He grants to one of His servants.

In the story of our master Jesus, peace be upon him: ﴿"I shall create for you from clay the likeness of a bird, then I breathe into it and it becomes a bird by God's permission.."﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 49].

The Qur'an responds to those who deny the resurrection, saying:

﴿We already know what the earth diminishes of them...﴾.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 50, verse 4:

Meaning: Why do you marvel at and deny resurrection after death, when Allah knows your constituent elements, the particles and components of this body, and the quantity of each element in it? He knows what the earth takes from you, and He is able to gather it and restore it as it was in its first creation, the very same, even though the elements that have left it are still outside it. Thus, we differ by the difference of the elements of composition, not by the difference of the sum of the elements.

The meaning of ﴿قَدْ عَلِمْنَا..﴾ [Qaf: 4] ("We have indeed known...") is that this process rests upon knowledge and understanding, not mere speech. It then rests upon another documentation: ﴿وَعِندَنَا كِتَابٌ حَفِيظٌ﴾ ("And with Us is a preserving Book") [Qaf: 4]. This knowledge is thus confirmed by a recorded, written, witnessed book in which everything is counted.

If you ask: what is the benefit of the Book after the knowledge? We say: Allah's knowledge is vast, and it is one of His attributes, and He, glorified is He, does not forget. But it is written in a book so that the book may be a proof against the one who denied, as in the matter of good deeds and bad deeds.

So Allah, exalted is He, knows them and counts them, and He has no need of anyone to remind Him of them; but He writes them for the servant so that they may be a proof against him on the day when it is said to him: ﴿اقْرَأْ كِتَابَكَ كَفَىٰ بِنَفْسِكَ الْيَوْمَ عَلَيْكَ حَسِيباً﴾ ("Read your record; sufficient is your soul against you this Day as a reckoner") [al-Isra: 14].

The word ﴿حَفِيظٌ﴾ [Qaf: 4] ("preserver") is an intensive form on the pattern fa'il, and here it carries the sense of fa'il (active participle). That is: He preserves everything, recording every small and great thing. And He Himself is preserved, so no hand can reach it to snatch anything from it or alter anything in it.

Therefore He said: ﴿إِنَّهُ لَقُرْآنٌ كَرِيمٌ * فِي كِتَابٍ مَّكْنُونٍ * لاَّ يَمَسُّهُ إِلاَّ الْمُطَهَّرُونَ﴾ ("Indeed, it is an honoured Qur'an, in a Book well-guarded, which none touches except the purified") [al-Waqi'a: 77–79].

And He said: ﴿وَعِندَهُ مَفَاتِحُ الْغَيْبِ لاَ يَعْلَمُهَا إِلاَّ هُوَ وَيَعْلَمُ مَا فِي الْبَرِّ وَالْبَحْرِ وَمَا تَسْقُطُ مِن وَرَقَةٍ إِلاَّ يَعْلَمُهَا وَلاَ حَبَّةٍ فِي ظُلُمَاتِ الأَرْضِ وَلاَ رَطْبٍ وَلاَ يَابِسٍ إِلاَّ فِي كِتَابٍ مُّبِينٍ﴾ ("With Him are the keys of the unseen; none knows them but He. He knows what is on the land and in the sea. Not a leaf falls but He knows it, nor a grain in the darknesses of the earth, nor anything moist or dry, but it is in a clear Book") [al-An'am: 59].

Those who try to cast doubt on resurrection or to refute it are the reckless people who are profligate against their own souls. For them, if resurrection is true and reckoning and recompense are true, the outcome will be black for them. Their interest, then, is to cast doubt on resurrection and to deny it; indeed, in their view the whole religion is falsehood.

Consider, for example, their bankruptcy of argument when they say in denying resurrection: If a man dies and an apple tree is planted over his remains, his elements will decompose and this tree will be nourished by them, and then someone will come and eat from it.

Thus some elements of the first will reach the second; when the second dies, how will these elements be resurrected, from the first or from the second?

This is a feeble doubt. In reply to it we say: If a man weighs, for example, a hundred kilos, and an illness reduces his weight by half until he becomes a shadow, then Allah bestows recovery upon him until he regains his health and his former weight, has the same elements of his first state returned to him?

Not at all, because he eats other elements, not those that left him. But the personality remains, and the distinctive characteristics of it remain, and when it returns, it returns as it was, the very same.

So the matter is not one of the same elements; it is a matter of re-creating a particular person. And since the Truth, glorified is He, has said: ﴿قَدْ عَلِمْنَا مَا تَنقُصُ الأَرْضُ مِنْهُمْ..﴾ ("We have indeed known what the earth diminishes of them...") [Qaf: 4], He, glorified is He, is able to gather them and form them anew, by His saying, exalted is He: "Be, and it is."

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 50, verse 5:

We understand from their saying: ﴿When we die and become dust, that is a far-off return﴾ [Qaf: 3] that they deny the resurrection, not believing that they will be raised after death. This denial changes nothing of the reality: the resurrection is true and will happen, but they deny it because it is not in their interest.

Therefore He said here: ﴿Nay, they have denied the truth when it came to them..﴾ [Qaf: 5]. Al-Haqq (the truth) is the thing that is established and never changes, no matter what events befall it. Events and occurrences will pass, and the truth will remain firm.

Allah, glory be to Him, gave us a tangible example of the truth and falsehood, saying: ﴿He sends down water from the sky, so the valleys flow according to their measure, and the torrent carries a swelling foam. And from what they smelt in the fire, seeking ornament or goods, there is a foam like it. Thus Allah strikes the example of truth and falsehood. As for the foam, it passes away as scum; but as for that which benefits mankind, it remains on the earth. Thus Allah sets forth the parables﴾ [Ar-Ra'd: 17].

Likewise their denial and rejection will go away, and the reality will remain, and the truth will remain firm and unchanging. In the Qur'an there are many verses carrying this meaning. Read: ﴿And He made the word of those who disbelieved the lowest, while the word of Allah is the highest..﴾ [At-Tawbah: 40]. Here the first (kalimah) is the object, while the second is the subject (mubtada') beginning a new statement, not conjoined to the first.

So the first is something made (majool), while the second is a matter fixed from eternity. He made the word of those who disbelieved the lowest, and the word of Allah the highest from the beginning; that is, it was not lowest and then He made it highest. This means that the truth is something fixed from eternity, enduring and unchanging.

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So they are in a confused matter﴾ [Qaf: 5]. The meaning of marij is mixed up, i.e., they are wavering and hesitant: at one time they marvelled and said ﴿This is a strange thing﴾ [Qaf: 2], at another time they denied, and at another time they called it a lie. The matter for them is mixed up, from their saying: marija al-khatim fi al-isba' (the ring became loose on the finger) when it was wide and easy to move.

The evidence that they are in a confused matter is that they confronted the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with a set of accusations; whenever their effort failed with one, they turned to another, because the Qur'an lies in wait for them, repelling their plots against the Messenger of Allah.

Therefore we have heard them say: a sorcerer, a poet, a madman, a soothsayer.

So: ﴿So they are in a confused matter﴾ [Qaf: 5] — they do not know what they are saying. Whenever they uttered an accusation, the Qur'an exposed its falsehood. The truth is one thing, therefore we see it firm; but falsehood is multiple, therefore it does not endure.

We witness this matter in testimony before a judge: the testimony of the truthful witness comes out one and unchanging, because it describes a reality; but the false witness changes and does not hold up before the judge's questioning, and soon he falls and his lie is exposed, because he does not describe a reality but fabricates events from himself.

Then Allah, glory be to Him and exalted, shifts the discourse to the cosmic signs that prove the power of Allah and touch on the matter of creed. When we correct their creed for them and turn them toward faith in Allah, they will reflect on the message of Muhammad and be guided to the truth.

Therefore He left off speaking of their denial of the Messenger of Allah and of the resurrection, and turned to speaking of the cosmic signs in the heavens and the earth.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 50, verses 6–8:

The interrogative in ﴿Have they not looked...﴾ [Qaf: 6] is intended to urge reflection and contemplation on the creation of the heavens and what they contain of signs and marvels, because these signs are evidence of power. The word ﴿We built it...﴾ [Qaf: 6] indicates that the sky, despite its vastness, is constructed, and despite the vastness of this structure, we see no pillars holding it up.

Therefore the Exalted said in another verse: ﴿It is Allah who raised the heavens without pillars that you can see﴾ [al-Ra'd: 2]. Thus, since there are no pillars bearing it, it is held up from above, and nothing holds this sky except a great power, the power of Allah: ﴿Indeed, Allah holds the heavens and the earth lest they cease [moving]﴾ [Fatir: 41].

We have seen this idea in the construction of long bridges that have no foundations and pillars to bear them; they are suspended from above, and these are called suspension bridges.

The Truth, glorified and exalted is He, brings this matter closer to us in His saying: ﴿Have they not considered the birds above them, spreading their wings and folding them in? None holds them up except the Most Merciful. Indeed, He is Seeing of all things﴾ [al-Mulk: 19]. Just as the bird is held up in the sky, so the heavens are held up from falling upon the earth except by His permission.

Then the matter does not stop at the construction of the sky; rather, ﴿We adorned it...﴾ [Qaf: 6] with what is in it of stars and planets that give light, ﴿and there are no cracks in it﴾ [Qaf: 6], meaning: there are no fissures or breaks in it. Rather, we see it level and smooth. Look at it when it is clear and you will find the splendor of its colors.

After He has told us of the sublime signs in the sky, He tells us of His signs on the earth. If the signs in the sky are far from us, the signs on the earth are near to us and within our perception.

﴿And the earth—We spread it out...﴾ [Qaf: 7]: We extended it and made it level and fit for habitation. Al-madd is spreading out, and a thing that is spread out and extended has no end. This is the attribute of the earth: wherever you travel, you find it stretching before you, with no edge where it ends. This extension has explained to us the roundness of the earth.

﴿And We placed firm mountains in it...﴾ [Qaf: 7]: these are the stable mountains that anchor the earth so that it does not sway, as He, glorified, said: ﴿And the mountains as stakes﴾ [al-Naba': 7], meaning the mountains are to the earth like the tent-pegs to a tent. ﴿And We caused to grow in it...﴾ [Qaf: 7], i.e., in the earth, ﴿of every beautiful pair﴾ [Qaf: 7] of plants. The word zawj (pair) means a kind, and it is an individual with its like.

Plants, in order to yield produce, must have two sexes, male and female, as in humans and animals. Therefore the Exalted said: ﴿And of everything We created pairs﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 49], because reproduction is not completed except by both.

It is known that pollination in plants is accomplished through butterflies and flying insects that carry pollen from the male element to the female element. So when insects multiplied in one of the orchards, they placed insecticide for them and they died. They noticed that the trees in the orchard did not blossom nor bear fruit. Why? Because the butterflies and insects that pollinate the crops had died.

They have also observed that insects take on the color of the flower they pollinate, so that there is a wonderful harmony of colors between them; you can hardly see the butterfly while it is on the flower. These colors in their harmony are a manifestation of the aspects of creative artistry.

As for His saying ﴿beautiful [bahij]﴾ [Qaf: 7]: it means lovely and pleasing in appearance.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 50, verses 9–10:

His words:

﴿And We sent down...﴾ [Qaf: 9]. The root n-z-l occurs in the forms anzalna and nazzalna. Anzalna is used for a thing that descends all at once, as in His words: ﴿Indeed, We sent it down during the Night of Decree﴾ [al-Qadr: 1], meaning: We sent it down on that night in its entirety. Then the Trustworthy Spirit brought it down piece by piece according to events, so He said: ﴿The Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down, upon your heart﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 193–194].

Likewise, water does not descend from the sky all at once; it descends in succession and in portions. So He said: ﴿And We sent down﴾ [Qaf: 9]. His words ﴿from the sky﴾ [Qaf: 9] mean: from the direction of the sky, because rain is in the clouds, and its origin is water from the salt water on the earth, where the process of evaporation takes place and the vapour of water condenses in the clouds, so the water is formed, which God Most High drives by the force of the wind, and it descends whenever it meets cold places.

And He described it as ﴿blessed water﴾ [Qaf: 9], because God has blessed it and made it fit for drinking and for irrigating plants; it is sweet, wholesome for those who drink.

When this blessed water descends upon the earth, the earth stirs and brings forth what is in it of plants: ﴿So We caused to grow thereby gardens﴾ [Qaf: 9]. Gardens is the plural of jannah, which is a place full of trees that conceal whoever walks among them; that is, they cover him, and so it is called jannah. From the same root is His words: ﴿When the night covered him﴾ [al-An'am: 76], meaning: it covered him with its darkness.

The meaning of ﴿and grain of harvest﴾ [Qaf: 9] is the grain that is reaped, such as wheat, barley, maize and rice. It is sown every year and harvested to be sown again. As for the gardens, they are lasting trees that live for many years and bear fruit, so one gathers only the fruit from them, and the tree remains as it is for the following year.

His words ﴿And the tall palm trees﴾ [Qaf: 10] mean: lofty and high. Height in the palm is among the wonders of creation and the precision of its design, for we have seen storms uproot some huge trees, but we have never seen a palm tree fall suddenly from a storm as a tree falls. Rather, when a palm tree weakens, we see it lean little by little at intervals until it reaches the ground. In it there is dignity and in it there is majesty.

God Most High mentioned the palm after the trees of the gardens and the grain of harvest because the palm combines both qualities: it gives its fruit every year like the trees, and yet, if it is not pollinated, the dates come as they say: ṣayṣ, meaning unripe dates that are of no benefit and have no use, so they are cut off and thrown away.

The meaning of ﴿it has spathes, layered﴾ [Qaf: 10]: the spathe (ṭalʿ) is a green sheath that splits open, and from it comes the spadix (subāṭa), which holds the strands (shamārīkh) that bear the dates. Among the wonders of creation is that you see these dates arranged in layers, that is, set in precise order on the strand that carries them, so that you will not find, for example, one date directly in front of another, but they are spread evenly along the strand in the shape of a crow's foot, as they say.

So: God Most High has given us a portion of His signs in the heavens and the earth, and we have said that the heavens and the earth are a container for what is in them. Despite the greatness of the creation of the heavens and the earth, what is contained within them is greater.

Man, in this containment, has a particularity, because he is God's vicegerent on earth. Regarding being contained, people are equal: none of them has a greater share than another, for they are equal in this containment, since the function of a container is to protect what is in it. A banknote of fifty stands equal in protection with one of a hundred, and gold, silver and iron are equal, for protection is for all, even though what is protected differs.

Likewise, man has his share of protection, although people's worth differs, and this difference came for a wisdom that God Most High intended for the benefit of the whole society: ﴿And We raised some of them above others in rank, that some of them may take others in service﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 32].

Among people there are the strong and the weak, the rich and the poor, the learned and the ignorant, the clever and the dull, and there is complementarity among them in the movement of life. We have said: what if all people graduated from university? Who then would do the lowly work? Therefore there must be people at the top and people beneath them for service, otherwise the movement of life would not be upright.

Yet despite this difference in worth, in terms of each person's work and his excellence in his work, we all remain the dependents and servants of God; none of us is the son of God. Let each of us keep to his manners and limits, for each of us is elevated in one matter and exalted over in another matter. That is to say: (no one is better than anyone else).

God Most High says:

﴿A provision for the servants; and We gave life thereby...﴾.

It is a provision for all of Allah's servants, believers and disbelievers, the obedient and the disobedient, because He created them all, and He must provide for those whom He created with the sustenance by which they live, even if they do not believe in Him, glorified is He.

When water descends upon it, it is revived with plant growth, as in the words of the Most High: ﴿And you see the earth lifeless, but when We send down upon it water, it stirs and swells and grows every lovely kind of plant﴾ [al-Hajj: 5].

The Most High has made the revival of dead land a proof and a living example of resurrection and return after death. He said: ﴿Thus will be the emergence﴾ [Qaf: 11]. This is similar to His words: ﴿And He who sends down water from the sky in measure, and We revive thereby a dead land. Thus you will be brought out﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 11].

It is also like His words: ﴿He brings the living out of the dead and brings the dead out of the living, and He revives the earth after its death. And thus will you be brought forth﴾ [al-Rum: 19], meaning: in the likeness of that you will be brought out and resurrected. Whoever denies resurrection should observe the process of the revival of the lifeless earth with plants after rain falls upon it. The earth is dead, lifeless and barren, with no trace of life in it. But when water descends upon it and rain waters it, it moves, stirs and grows, and the cracks in the soil that were caused by thirst are closed, and then it sprouts every lovely kind. It is thus a living, observable model of creation and of life.

This is consolation for the Messenger of God, and a lightening of what he meets from his people's denial of him. The verses first presented their attitude: ﴿Nay, they wonder that a warner has come to them from among themselves﴾ [Qaf: 2], then they denied the resurrection that he had told them of, saying: ﴿When we have died and become dust—that is a far-off return﴾ [Qaf: 3].

So the Truth, glory be to Him, wished to show His Messenger the procession of the messages before him, and how much denial of his brother messengers had occurred in them.

It is as if He says to him: O Muhammad, you are no novelty in this. ﴿Before them denied [the messengers]...﴾ [Qaf: 12], i.e., before your people, ﴿the people of Noah...﴾ [Qaf: 12], although he remained among them a thousand years less fifty years, and despite that they denied and none believed with him except a few of them.

But did God leave them? No, rather He took vengeance upon them with the drowning that annihilated them to the last one. The Truth, glory be to Him, would not leave the people of corruption, the people of denial and of confronting the messengers, without punishment; rather He gives them respite and then seizes them without leniency.

The people of Noah, peace be upon him, used to mock him while he was building the ship, and he would say to them: "A day will come when we will mock you just as you mock us," as if he were certain of God's victory and support for his call. And just as the people of Noah denied, so did ﴿the companions of the Rass...﴾ [Qaf: 12].

Al-Rass (the well) is the name of a well known [to them]. ﴿And Thamud﴾ [Qaf: 12], and they are the people of our master Salih. ﴿And ʿAd﴾ [Qaf: 13], the people of our master Hud. ﴿And Pharaoh...﴾ [Qaf: 13].

The story of Pharaoh with our master Musa is well known. ﴿And the brothers of Lot...﴾ [Qaf: 13], i.e., his people. ﴿And the companions of al-Aykah...﴾ [Qaf: 14]. Al-Aykah is the dense garden of intertwined trees and tangled branches, and the inhabitants of this garden were the people of our master Shu'ayb.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 50, verse 15:

The context here returns to discussing those who deny resurrection, who said: ﴿When we have died and become dust, that is a far return.﴾ [Qaf: 3] It returns to this subject to say to them: Why do you deny resurrection? Do you not have before you the first creation? ﴿Were We then wearied by the first creation?﴾ [Qaf: 15] That is: Did We become incapable of it, did it tire Us? No, rather We were able to do it and brought it into being from non-existence.

The first creation is the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the creation of the first human being, Adam (peace be upon him). The One who is able to create at the beginning is able to recreate by even greater right.

﴿Nay, but they are in confusion about a new creation.﴾ [Qaf: 15] That is: in mixture and hesitation, as He said about them in the previous verses: ﴿So they are in a confused matter.﴾ [Qaf: 5] That is: mixed up.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 50, verse 16:

After He, glorified is He, spoke to us of His cosmic signs in the heavens and the earth, He speaks to us of His signs in the creation of man. Al-Haqq, glorified is He, has made clear that the signs of the heavens and the earth are greater than the signs that are in the creation of people. ﴿The creation of the heavens and the earth is greater than the creation of mankind...﴾ [Ghafir: 57]. He, glorified is He, promised us with His saying ﴿We will show them Our signs in the horizons...﴾ [Fussilat: 53], the horizons of the heavens and the earth, ﴿and within themselves, until it becomes clear to them that it is the truth...﴾ [Fussilat: 53].

He, glorified is He, says: ﴿And We have certainly created man...﴾ [Qaf: 16]. He reinforced the statement for them with (al-lam) and (qad) because they deny this truth and reject it, and this denial is a form of obstinate rejection on their part, since He said in another place: ﴿And if you asked them who created them, they would surely say, "Allah"﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 87].

Since al-Haqq, glorified is He, has said ﴿And We have certainly created man...﴾ [Qaf: 16], it is not possible to say that it is conceivable for man to be cloned. The man who forms a family of a father and a mother cannot ever be cloned; only the One who created him can recreate him.

The proof is that He created Adam and took from him a rib from which He made Hawwa'. As for you, you will not be able to do this. You may be able to clone a plant or an animal, for these creatures are not required to form a family.

What is required of a plant or an animal is only reproduction, whereas man is not required only to reproduce, but is also required to uphold values as a being in society.

Man strives to form a family and has specific qualities in the one he marries, and how they live together, each of them performing a task in upbringing that suits them. He toils outside the house, and she carries out her task in the house, and her task is higher and more important than his.

Therefore we find the foundling (laqit) miserable in his life, because he has no father to whom he is attributed; whereas one who has a father, his son is reckoned to him and is held responsible for him before society, and he provides for his livelihood and education. So if we supposed that it were possible for there to be a cloned human being, how would his life be?

Allah is the Creator of man and his Originator, and the Creator is the most knowing of whom He has created, and the most knowing of their secrets and what is good for them. ﴿And We know what his soul whispers to him...﴾ [Qaf: 16]. That is: We do not know merely the outward aspects of his deeds, but We know their inner aspects, and We know what stirs in his soul of thoughts and ideas. ﴿Should not He who created know? And He is the Subtle, the All-Aware﴾ [Al-Mulk: 14].

He who knows the subtleties and hidden depths of matters, like the craftsman who knows the fine details of his craft. For example, when your watch stops working, you know nothing about it, so you take it to the watchmaker, and as soon as he looks at it he knows where the fault is and repairs it with a very simple movement.

So al-Haqq, glorified is He, created man, and man is His craft and His originating. Therefore He knows the hidden depths of his soul, not merely the outward aspects of his deeds, because the outward aspects of deeds are known to people, so there is no merit in knowing them. But what the soul whispers is an unseen matter for others, which no one perceives or knows except Allah, and this is among the signs of Allah within the selves: ﴿We will show them Our signs in the horizons and within themselves...﴾ [Fussilat: 53].

He called the thoughts that come to the mind waswasa (whispering), which in origin is the sound of jewelry (al-hilyy), and whispering comes sometimes from the self (nafs) and sometimes from Satan, so it is only ever for evil. The Imam ʿAli (ʿalayhi al-salam) explained the difference between them when a questioner asked him: How do I know the source of this whispering, is it from the self or from Satan?

He replied: The self stops you at one specific sin and does not budge from it, whereas Satan wants you to be disobedient in whatever form it may be; if you oppose him in one sin, he makes another one attractive to you, and so on until he brings you down.

The self is the root of whispering, for if we take the first disobedience of Iblis and ask, who whispered it to him? His own self. And the poet, when he versified this meaning, said: When Iblis disobeyed, who was his Iblis?

So the matter, then, goes back to the self, and Iblis exploits the desire of the self, nourishes it, and makes it attractive to its owner. And strangely, these whisperings, when they press upon a person, drown him in worries and imaginings that have no basis, so he occupies himself with things that have not happened but which he imagines have happened, or with past events that he replays anew.

Thus worries besiege him; you speak to him and find him absent-minded, or he walks while talking to himself. The intelligent person (al-'aqil) is the one who does not leave his self prey to these whisperings, and knows that he has a Lord who knows what his self whispers.

A generous Lord who relieves distresses and removes worries. The intelligent person is one who knows that what has passed is gone, the expected is unseen, and you have only the hour you are in.

It is the nature of the believer to have a reserve of faith that protects him. If means become scarce for him, he turns to the One who causes causes, so he never despairs and never gives in.

We have said: If a man has only one pound (junayh) and loses it, he will surely grieve, especially if he is a stranger, for example. But if you lose a pound and there are ten in the house, the grief is less. So what of it if you have a reserve from the Lord of the worlds?

Therefore they say: "No distress, for you have a Lord." This reserve of faith we saw in the story of our master Musa, peace be upon him, when his means were constrained and he said: ﴿He said, "No! Indeed, with me is my Lord; He will guide me."﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara': 62].

And His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And We are closer to him than the jugular vein﴾ [Qaf: 16]. Habl al-warid (the jugular vein) is two veins in the neck that carry nourishment to the whole body, and when the jugular vein is cut, life ends. The statement here is an allusion (kinaya) to the nearness of al-Haqq, glorified is He, to His servant, as if He were saying to him: I am near you and I know your details, and I know the whisperings of your self.

Almighty God has made clear that His knowledge encompasses everything: He does not merely know the deeds of the limbs, but He knows what passes through the soul, its inner stirrings and thoughts, before they are translated into action. Therefore, knowledge of the whispering of the soul (al-waswasa) is more fitting than knowledge of the limbs and their deeds. But the servant may say: "I will hide, and no one will see me."

So God made clear to him that if he hides from people, he does not hide from God, and his deeds are not concealed from the two noble recording angels (al-malakayn al-katibayn) who receive his deeds and preserve them: an angel on his right who records the good deeds, and an angel on his left who records the bad deeds.

The meaning of ﴿qa'id﴾ [Qaf: 17] is: each of them sits in wait for him, dedicated to him, watching him and never absent from him. ﴿Not a word does he utter but there is with him a watcher, ready [to record]﴾ [Qaf: 18]. If you ask: since God knows the deeds of the servant, and nothing is hidden from Him, why then are his deeds written down and recorded against him?

They say: deeds are recorded so that they may serve as proof against their doer on the Day of Resurrection. Just as God will make the limbs speak to bear witness against their owner, so this record will also speak. Consider: ﴿On the Day when their tongues, their hands and their feet will bear witness against them concerning what they used to do﴾ [An-Nur: 24].

He, glorified is He, also said: ﴿And they will say to their skins, "Why did you testify against us?" They will say, "We were made to speak by Allah, who made everything speak"﴾ [Fussilat: 21], and He said: ﴿This is Our record; it speaks against you with the truth﴾ [Al-Jathiya: 29].

Among God's mercy to His servants in the recording of deeds is that the guardian angels record a good deed as ten times its like, while they record an evil deed as only one. A good deed is recorded merely by your intending it, whereas an evil deed is not recorded until you actually commit it. Moreover, He gives you an opportunity, perhaps you will repent or reconsider yourself.

Meaning of: ﴿The agony of death...﴾ [Qaf: 19]: its overwhelming, or the state of unconsciousness that seizes a person at the time of the death-rattle (ghargharah) and the departure of the soul. It is called "the agony of death" (sakrat al-mawt, lit. the intoxication of death) because it is the prelude to death. And His saying: ﴿with truth...﴾ [Qaf: 19], because the truth is death. It is a truth that is obligatory for every creature, and an arrow released toward every newborn, and your lifespan is according to the measure of its arrival at you.

Therefore a person dies as a fetus, dies as a child, dies as a youth, and dies as an old man.

Among the signs of God regarding death is that He made it indefinite in time and indefinite in place, and this indefiniteness is the clearest explanation, for indefiniteness makes you await it at every moment, and makes you prepare for it through repentance and righteous deeds. It makes you feel shame before God that death should overtake you while you are in disobedience.

And His saying: ﴿That...﴾ [Qaf: 19], i.e., death, ﴿is what you used to shun﴾ [Qaf: 19], i.e., you used to incline away from it and fear it. Indeed, all of us fear death and keep it away from ourselves, imagining that all people will die except him.

Therefore it is related in the hadith: ... and keeping away from the specter of death is a wisdom willed by the Truth, glory be to Him, for if each one of us truly kept in mind the reality of death, no life would be pleasant to him, nor would he find any settled rest, and no one would benefit from any deed.

So then: hope in life is the better course. Hope is what populates the movement of life; love of life is what drives us to build life. The important thing is that this hope does not make you forget death, so be ready for it through repentance and seeking forgiveness whenever a sin has come from you.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 50, verses 20–21:

Here he gives us a scene from the scenes of the Day of Judgment, the Day when the Trumpet (al-Sur) is blown. It is said: it is the second blast, by which people rise from their graves. The Sur is the horn into which Israfil (peace be upon him) blows.

﴿That is the day that was promised.﴾ [Qaf: 20] That is: the day that We promised you and warned you of. Al-wa'id (threat) is the opposite of al-wa'd (promise): al-wa'id is with evil that is coming, and al-wa'd is with good. Death is feared only by the one who has bad deeds, like the final exam of the year, which is feared only by the negligent student, whereas the diligent one rejoices in it.

Likewise, the one who has good deeds rejoices in meeting Allah, because he is heading toward the complete reward from Allah. Therefore, when a righteous man dies, we say: "O Allah, join us to him."

And His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And every soul will come, with it a driver and a witness.﴾ [Qaf: 21] A driver who drives it to the land of gathering, and a witness who testifies against it for what it did.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 50, verse 22:

﴿You were certainly heedless of this...﴾ [Qaf: 22] in heedlessness and forgetfulness of this Day. ﴿So We have removed from you your covering...﴾ [Qaf: 22] i.e., We have removed from you the covering of heedlessness.

﴿So your sight, this Day, is sharp﴾ [Qaf: 22] i.e., keen and penetrating, able to perceive matters as they truly are, i.e., the matters of the Hereafter and what is in them of resurrection, reckoning, and recompense.

Meaning of "his companion" (Qari'nuhu) [Qaf: 23]: that is the angel who accompanies him and is constantly with him, on his right and on his left, recording all his deeds and every breath he takes. He comes and says: "This is what I have ready (ʿatīd) with me." This is what I have recorded against this servant, prepared and ready.

Just as, for example, the police officer when he presents a report to the public prosecution, presenting the evidence and saying: "This is what I have; my task is finished, and the matter of judgement rests with the prosecution."

And His saying, exalted is He: "Cast into Hell every stubborn disbeliever" [Qaf: 24]: this is a command from the Truth, glory be to Him, to each of the driver and the witness that they cast into Hell every (disbeliever) who is intensely disbelieving and firmly established in it.

Disbelief (kufr) is either ingratitude for blessings (kufr al-niʿmah), as happened with the people of Sheba, concerning whom Allah said: "That is how We recompensed them for their disbelief" [Saba': 17], meaning they denied the blessing of Allah; or denial of the Benefactor, glory be to Him, which is disbelief in divinity (kufr al-ulūhiyyah).

The word "disbeliever" (kaffār) [Qaf: 24] is an intensive form of "kāfir." It does not mean one who disbelieved once, but rather one in whom disbelief is repeated; for this reason He described him afterwards as "stubborn" (ʿanīd) [Qaf: 24], meaning obstinate in his disbelief, insisting upon it and persisting in it.

Disbelief (kufr), linguistically, is concealment (al-satr). Ingratitude for blessings comes in two forms: concealing the blessing in its place, meaning that they did not come to it through the effort of work, striving and deduction; or that they gathered it and brought it into their pockets, then withheld it from the needy.

Likewise, the word "stubborn" (ʿanīd) [Qaf: 24] contains intensification: we say "muʿānid" and "ʿanīd." The stubborn one is he who opposes whenever you call him to the truth and insists upon his position. There is no doubt that the Messenger's call to people to believe is repeated constantly, but the stubborn one opposes it, does not accept it, and is not guided; he persists, clinging to his opinion, accepting no proof and accepting no debate.

So: disbelief in the blessing, and disbelief in the Benefactor.

And His saying, exalted is He: "Withholder of good, transgressor, doubter" [Qaf: 25]: this is the third attribute of the stubborn disbeliever. In addition to the severity of his disbelief and his obstinacy, he is "withholder of good" (mannāʿ lil-khayr) [Qaf: 25]. Mannāʿ is also an intensive form of māniʿ, so he is one who very much withholds good, withholding it even from himself after having withheld it from others, when he stood in the face of the call to faith, and when he withheld his wealth and did not give to the needy.

Then, after all of that, he is "transgressor, doubter" [Qaf: 25]. He was not content with withholding good, but he also encroached upon the good that belonged to others, taking it without right: once by theft, once by bribery, once by abduction and usurpation, once by deception, once by fraud... etc.

He is thus a transgressor in every way of transgression, and he is "doubter" (murīb) [Qaf: 25], meaning one who is in doubt and suspicion about this Day. Had he truly believed in it and in the reckoning and the recompense, he would not have done that; had he believed in the requital, he would have given and not withheld.

Among his attributes also is: "who set up with Allah another god" [Qaf: 26]. The error here is at the peak, in the matter of faith in Allah, and Allah says: "Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whomever He wills" [al-Nisaʾ: 116]. Therefore the recompense was: "So cast him into the severe punishment" [Qaf: 26].

So: we have two kinds of punishment: an unqualified punishment, not described as severe, in His saying: "Cast into Hell..." [Qaf: 24], and this is for one who disobeys Allah and commits major sins short of associating partners with Allah.

Then a punishment described as severe, for one who associates partners with Allah, exalted is He. This is because the perpetrator of a major sin utters "There is no god but Allah," and may repent, for the word of monotheism has an effect in protecting the soul, even in the sinner.

As for the polytheist, he does not utter the word of monotheism, and it has no effect on his soul. If we placed this with that, the word of monotheism would have no meaning and no effect.

This falls under His saying, exalted is He: "Except for those who repent and believe and do righteous deeds; for those, Allah will replace their evil deeds with good deeds..." [al-Furqan: 70].

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 50, verse 30:

Earlier in the verses, God Most High said: ﴿Cast into Hell every stubborn disbeliever﴾ [Qaf: 24]. Here, Allah the Glorified asks Hell: ﴿Has it been filled?﴾ [Qaf: 30]. Also, a promise was made earlier by God that He would fill Hell: ﴿I will surely fill Hell with jinn and mankind all together﴾ [As-Sajdah: 13].

So: this promise must be fulfilled for it. The question here, ﴿Has it been filled?﴾ [Qaf: 30], is a question seeking confirmation, and the answer comes: ﴿Is there any more?﴾ [Qaf: 30], meaning: it has been filled, yet it wants more. So where will You place them in it?

You remember that we said earlier that the Creator, Glorified is He, from eternity created Paradise to accommodate all of mankind if they believe, and created Hell to accommodate all of mankind if they disbelieve. Thus the places of the believers in Hell are left empty, and the places of the disbelievers in Paradise are left empty, so Hell says: ﴿Is there any more?﴾ [Qaf: 30], to fill the empty places in it.

After the verses spoke of Hell (may God protect us), they mention its counterpart, Paradise: ﴿And Paradise will be brought near﴾ [Qaf: 31], meaning it will be brought near to the God-fearing (al-muttaqun), because they were given good news of it in this world, and of the fact that God, exalted is He, does not break His promise.

As for now, in the situation of the Hereafter, it draws near to them ﴿not far off﴾ [Qaf: 31], meaning: it is brought near to them in a nearness that is not far.

This is the commentary of al-Sha'rawi on surah 50, verses 32–33:

The words of the Exalted, ﴿This is what you were promised﴾ [Qaf: 32], refer to what was mentioned earlier about the Garden being brought near to the God-fearing, ﴿what you were promised﴾ [Qaf: 32], meaning: what God promised it to be. ﴿For every penitent returner﴾ [Qaf: 32]. Awwab (penitent, one who constantly returns) is an intensive form. We say: a'ib (one who returns) and awwab, meaning one who frequently returns and turns back to God whenever he commits a sin, and who swiftly regrets it and repents.

The Exalted and Glorified has explained this meaning to us in His words: ﴿Repentance with God is only for those who do evil in ignorance...﴾ [An-Nisa: 17], meaning: they do not hasten towards it nor plan for it. ﴿Then they repent soon after; those are the ones to whom God turns in forgiveness, and God is ever Knowing and Wise. And repentance is not for those who do evil deeds until, when death approaches one of them, he says, "Indeed, I have repented now"...﴾ [An-Nisa: 17–18].

The awwab is one who frequently returns to God in repentance. This does not mean that he is one who has many sins; rather, if heedlessness of obedience occurs in him, he hastens to repentance. For the one who returns in repentance from a sin and then goes back to it, repeating this again and again, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) has compared him to one who mocks his Lord, and this is a quality that does not befit the awwab.

The meaning of ﴿Hafiz (one who guards)﴾ [Qaf: 32] is also an intensive form of hafiz (guardian). The hafiz is one who greatly guards the limits of God and the sanctities of God; he protects himself from falling into disobedience, and indeed protects himself from approaching it.

This is the meaning of the noble hadith: The guarding of God is by guarding His limits and standing at His commands and prohibitions.

Among the qualities of the God-fearing, to whom God has promised this promise, is ﴿whoever fears the Most Merciful in the unseen﴾ [Qaf: 33]. Khashyah (fear) means dread, and it is of two kinds: one is that you fear someone while you hate him and curse him, because he is stronger than you, or because he humiliates and subdues you, so you fear him and despise him. This is the fear of servants of servants.

And there is fear with love, reverence and awe, in the manner of the poet's saying:

I fear you out of reverence, though you have no power over me, but because your beloved's eye is full of you.

So you love the one you fear, knowing that he has favour upon you, and that you cannot fulfil his right. This is the fear of God. What helps us understand this meaning is the saying of God, the Exalted: ﴿Do you not see that God sends down water from the sky, and We produce thereby fruits of varying colours? And among the mountains are white and red streaks of varying shades, and some are intensely black. And among people and creatures and livestock are those of varying colours. Only those of His servants who have knowledge truly fear God...﴾ [Fatir: 27–28].

Here the Exalted has not brought a legal ruling that obliges us to it or frightens us from neglecting it; rather, He speaks of the signs of His creation, wishing us to ponder them and contemplate them, and to search out their secrets and the beauty within them.

Whenever we look at the signs of creation around us, our fear of God, and our awe and reverence for His greatness and His favour upon us, increase. The scholars are the most deserving of this contemplation, and the closest of people to fearing God and esteeming Him as He deserves.

Consider here the Qur'anic expression: ﴿whoever fears the Most Merciful in the unseen...﴾ [Qaf: 33]. He chose the attribute of mercy and did not say "whoever fears the Subduer or the Compeller," because the fear here is wrapped in love, mercy, glorification and reverence for God, whom we fear and dread.

Then He restricted this fear by saying ﴿in the unseen...﴾ [Qaf: 33], meaning: not displayed before people. The true believer fears God in his secret before his public, and in his solitude before his gatherings; he fears Him between himself and himself.

As for the weak in faith, he fears God in front of people, and when he is in a gathering of them he speaks of the lawful and the unlawful; but when he is alone with himself he violates the sanctities of God.

So his fear of God contains show-off and is mixed with association (shirk). Therefore He described the God-fearing and the people of the Garden as those who fear the Most Merciful in the unseen.

Among the meanings of "the unseen" is also that when the believer is warned of the punishment of God and the Fire is mentioned to him while he is still in the breadth of this world, he fears it, and believes in its existence though he has not seen it. This is fear in the unseen, because the Fire, for us now, is unseen, and we only affirm its existence because God has informed us of it.

The believer takes the report from God as though it were a reality he sees with his own eyes and touches with his senses; the report from God is more truthful than the sight of the eye. We explained this matter in the saying of God: ﴿Have you not seen how your Lord dealt with the companions of the elephant?﴾ [Al-Fil: 1].

Here the address is to our master, the Messenger of God, and he did not witness the incident of the elephant, for he was born that year. So why did He not address him by saying, "Do you not know," and turn away from that to, "Have you not seen?" They say: because the report from God is more truthful than the sight of the eye. Yes, because sight may deceive you, whereas God's report is absolute truth.

﴿And he comes with a repentant heart﴾ [Qaf: 33], meaning: a heart that is sincere to God and true in obedience. The heart is the seat of faith, and God, as we have mentioned, desires from us the heart and not the body; the body can be compelled to believe, but the heart does not come except through love and willing submission.

Therefore the Exalted made faith a matter of choice, with no compulsion in it. Had He willed, He would have compelled all creation to believe in Him, as He compelled the heavens and the earth; but He wished for His servants to come to Him willingly and with conviction.

The meaning of ﴿Hafiz (one who guards)﴾ [Qaf: 32] is also an intensive form of hafiz (guardian). The hafiz is one who greatly guards the limits of God and the sanctities of God; he protects himself from falling into disobedience, and indeed protects himself from approaching it.

This is the meaning of the noble hadith: The guarding of God is by guarding His limits and standing at His commands and prohibitions.

Among the qualities of the God-fearing, to whom God has promised this promise, is ﴿whoever fears the Most Merciful in the unseen﴾ [Qaf: 33]. Khashyah (fear) means dread, and it is of two kinds: one is that you fear someone while you hate him and curse him, because he is stronger than you, or because he humiliates and subdues you, so you fear him and despise him. This is the fear of servants of servants.

And there is fear with love, reverence and awe, in the manner of the poet's saying:

I fear you out of reverence, though you have no power over me, but because your beloved's eye is full of you.

So you love the one you fear, knowing that he has favour upon you, and that you cannot fulfil his right. This is the fear of God. What helps us understand this meaning is the saying of God, the Exalted: ﴿Do you not see that God sends down water from the sky, and We produce thereby fruits of varying colours? And among the mountains are white and red streaks of varying shades, and some are intensely black. And among people and creatures and livestock are those of varying colours. Only those of His servants who have knowledge truly fear God...﴾ [Fatir: 27–28].

Here the Exalted has not brought a legal ruling that obliges us to it or frightens us from neglecting it; rather, He speaks of the signs of His creation, wishing us to ponder them and contemplate them, and to search out their secrets and the beauty within them.

Whenever we look at the signs of creation around us, our fear of God, and our awe and reverence for His greatness and His favour upon us, increase. The scholars are the most deserving of this contemplation, and the closest of people to fearing God and esteeming Him as He deserves.

Consider here the Qur'anic expression: ﴿whoever fears the Most Merciful in the unseen...﴾ [Qaf: 33]. He chose the attribute of mercy and did not say "whoever fears the Subduer or the Compeller," because the fear here is wrapped in love, mercy, glorification and reverence for God, whom we fear and dread.

Then He restricted this fear by saying ﴿in the unseen...﴾ [Qaf: 33], meaning: not displayed before people. The true believer fears God in his secret before his public, and in his solitude before his gatherings; he fears Him between himself and himself.

As for the weak in faith, he fears God in front of people, and when he is in a gathering of them he speaks of the lawful and the unlawful; but when he is alone with himself he violates the sanctities of God.

So his fear of God contains show-off and is mixed with association (shirk). Therefore He described the God-fearing and the people of the Garden as those who fear the Most Merciful in the unseen.

Among the meanings of "the unseen" is also that when the believer is warned of the punishment of God and the Fire is mentioned to him while he is still in the breadth of this world, he fears it, and believes in its existence though he has not seen it. This is fear in the unseen, because the Fire, for us now, is unseen, and we only affirm its existence because God has informed us of it.

The believer takes the report from God as though it were a reality he sees with his own eyes and touches with his senses; the report from God is more truthful than the sight of the eye. We explained this matter in the saying of God: ﴿Have you not seen how your Lord dealt with the companions of the elephant?﴾ [Al-Fil: 1].

Here the address is to our master, the Messenger of God, and he did not witness the incident of the elephant, for he was born that year. So why did He not address him by saying, "Do you not know," and turn away from that to, "Have you not seen?" They say: because the report from God is more truthful than the sight of the eye. Yes, because sight may deceive you, whereas God's report is absolute truth.

﴿And he comes with a repentant heart﴾ [Qaf: 33], meaning: a heart that is sincere to God and true in obedience. The heart is the seat of faith, and God, as we have mentioned, desires from us the heart and not the body; the body can be compelled to believe, but the heart does not come except through love and willing submission.

Therefore the Exalted made faith a matter of choice, with no compulsion in it. Had He willed, He would have compelled all creation to believe in Him, as He compelled the heavens and the earth; but He wished for His servants to come to Him willingly and with conviction.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 50, verses 34–35:

That is: enter Paradise "in peace" (Qur'an 50:34), a peace free of all disturbances, and you will never be moved to grief or constriction after that. This statement, "enter it in peace," is the saying of the angels when they greet them with peace.

Likewise, the Truth, glory be to Him, says it to them in His saying: "Peace, a word from a Lord, Most Merciful" (Qur'an 36:58). Whoever meets his Lord with peace, there is no misery for him after that, ever.

Or, "enter it in peace" means: greeting one another, saying to your brethren, "Peace be upon you," just as you used to greet them and salute them with it in the world. Likewise in the Hereafter you will salute with it the Keeper (Malik) at the gate of Paradise, and salute your brethren with it.

"That is the Day of Eternity" (Qur'an 50:34): "That" refers to the Day of Resurrection. "The Day of Eternity" is the day of permanence, continuance, and bliss that does not end and does not pass away. This is the difference between the bliss of this world and the bliss of the Hereafter.

Whatever the bliss of this world may be, it is troubled for its possessor by two things: that the bliss is lost by death, or that he is deprived of it by poverty or sickness. But the bliss of the Hereafter is safe from every disturbance.

As for the saying of the Exalted: "For them is whatever they will therein" (Qur'an 50:35), that is: in Paradise. The orientalists have stopped at this verse, saying: how can it be established for them to have a will regarding what they desire, when it has been reported that "will" means they know what they desire?

They said: they will what they knew and took pleasure in of the bliss of this world, whereas the bliss of the Hereafter is entirely different from it; they have of it only the names, while the reality of the thing differs. Therefore He said after it: "And with Us is more" (Qur'an 50:35).

The Truth, glory be to Him, explained this matter in His saying: "And give good tidings to those who believe and do righteous deeds, that for them are gardens beneath which rivers flow. Whenever they are provided with a fruit therefrom as provision, they say, 'This is what we were provided with before,' and they are given it in resemblance..." (Qur'an 2:25).

That is: if his soul longs, for example, to eat a mango, he finds it different from what he knew in the world; if he asks for it the next day, he finds it different from the one he ate on the first day, and so on. They are similar, but not the same.

So: He gave them a will regarding what they know of the bliss of this world and what they desire from it. But in the Hereafter it is something else, as evidence: when you desire something you ask for it by its name, and the name is a branch of knowing the meaning; and since those things are strange to us, we therefore do not know them and do not know a name for them.
